entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Slower than others to understand or adapt to new developments, so that you fall behind them.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and economic news, usually as a criticism: *be behind the curve on* something. In economics it often describes a central bank that reacts too late to inflation. The opposite, *ahead of the curve*, is praise for seeing a trend early.
entries.pattern: be / fall behind the curve (on something)
examples: Most newspapers were **behind the curve** on the internet and lost their classified ads to sites like Craigslist.
Critics say the Fed was **behind the curve** on inflation and raised rates too late.
My parents are a bit **behind the curve** with technology; they just discovered group texts.

drill.sentence: Our town was way {{behind the curve}} on recycling; most cities nearby had curbside pickup ten years before we did.
drill.hint: slower than others to adapt (not *… the times*)

entries.related: *ahead of the curve* — the opposite, early to see a trend; *behind the times* — old-fashioned in general; *play catch-up* — try to reach others after falling behind.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: As good as the normal or expected standard.
entries.usage: Mostly used in the negative or in questions: *not up to par*, *Is it up to par?* It is a mild way to say that work, service or performance was worse than usual, and *not feeling up to par* means slightly unwell. *Up to snuff* means the same and sounds more casual.
examples: The food at that diner used to be great, but lately it hasn't been **up to par**.
I've had a cold all week, so I'm still not feeling **up to par**.
The inspector said the wiring wasn't **up to par** and refused to sign off on the house.

drill.sentence: The coach benched him for two games because his effort in practice wasn't {{up to par}}.
drill.hint: good enough by the usual standard (not *snuff* or *scratch*)

entries.related: *up to snuff* — same, more casual; *up to scratch* — same, more common in British English; *subpar* — below the expected standard.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of an argument, an excuse or a theory: to be unconvincing or illogical once you examine it closely.
entries.usage: Used about excuses, alibis, claims and arguments in conversation, journalism and law. It is almost always negative or in a question: *doesn't hold water*, *won't hold water*, *Does that hold water?* The subject is the idea, not the person: *His story doesn't hold water.*
examples: She said she was home all night, but her story **doesn't hold water**; her car was seen downtown.
The idea that a supplement is safe just because it's natural **doesn't hold water**.
The claim that the new model generalizes better **won't hold water**; it was tested on only one dataset.

drill.sentence: My son says he couldn't do his homework because the Wi-Fi was down, but that excuse {{doesn't hold water}}; he was gaming online all evening.
drill.hint: is not convincing once you check it (not *add up* or *fly*)

entries.related: *not add up* — have facts that don't fit together; *not stand up to scrutiny* — more formal; *be full of holes* — have many weak points.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a decision based on your instinct or feeling instead of on careful analysis.
entries.usage: Common advice in conversation when someone can't decide: *Just go with your gut.* It suggests that your first feeling is probably right and that more thinking won't help. *Trust your gut* means the same, and *my gut tells me* introduces an instinct.
examples: I couldn't decide between the two apartments, so I **went with my gut** and picked the one with more light.
On multiple-choice tests, I usually **go with my gut** instead of changing my first answer.
Experienced ER nurses learn when to **go with their gut** about a patient who seems fine on paper.

drill.sentence: Everyone told me to take the higher-paying job, but I {{went with my gut}} and stayed in Denver, and I'm glad I did.
drill.hint: followed my instinct, a feeling in the stomach (not *trusted …*)

entries.related: *trust your gut* — same; *sleep on it* — wait a night before deciding; *overthink it* — the opposite habit.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To decide what to do as the situation develops, instead of making a fixed plan in advance.
entries.usage: Very common in casual planning, often as a friendly way to avoid committing: *Let's just play it by ear.* The object is usually just *it*. It sounds relaxed, but to someone who likes clear plans it can sound vague.
examples: We don't know what the weather will do, so let's **play it by ear** and decide on the beach tomorrow morning.
With two toddlers, we never make dinner reservations anymore; we just **play it by ear**.
My boss said we'd **play it by ear** on whether the office reopens after the holidays.

drill.sentence: I'm not sure when I'll get off work on Friday, so let's {{play it by ear}} and text each other around six.
drill.hint: decide later as things develop (not *see how it goes*)

entries.related: *wing it* — improvise without any preparation; *see how it goes* — plainer; *take it as it comes* — deal with things as they happen.
entries.origin: From music: playing a tune by listening and remembering it, without reading the notes.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Spoken or done without preparation or notes, on the spot.
entries.usage: Used mainly about speaking: remarks, comments, speeches and answers. After a verb it has no hyphens (*speak off the cuff*); before a noun it does (*an off-the-cuff remark*). An off-the-cuff comment is often one that the speaker later regrets or has to explain.
examples: The best man didn't write anything down; he spoke **off the cuff** and had everyone laughing.
The CEO later apologized for an **off-the-cuff** remark about employees who work from home.
I can't give you exact numbers **off the cuff**, but I'll email them to you this afternoon.

drill.sentence: She hadn't planned to speak at the funeral, but she stood up and shared a few memories {{off the cuff}}.
drill.hint: without any preparation (a shirt image)

entries.related: *ad-lib* — improvise words, especially on stage; *on the spot* — immediately, without time to think; *wing it* — do something without preparation.
entries.origin: Probably from the idea of a speaker glancing at a few notes written on a shirt cuff.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To surprise someone at a moment when they are not prepared, so that they don't know how to react.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news, often in the passive: *I was caught off guard by the question.* It works for questions, news, attacks and kind gestures alike. Compared with *surprise*, it stresses that the person wasn't ready to respond.
entries.pattern: catch someone off guard / be caught off guard (by something)
examples: The question about my salary **caught me off guard**, and for a moment I just stared at her.
The early snowstorm **caught the city off guard**; half the plows weren't ready.
I was **caught off guard** when my brother announced at dinner that he was moving to Japan.

drill.sentence: The ending of the movie really {{caught me off guard}}; I never saw that twist coming.
drill.hint: surprised me when I wasn't ready (not *took … by surprise*)

entries.related: *take someone by surprise* — similar, with less focus on being unready; *blindside* — hit someone with a harmful surprise, mainly American.

entries.term: like a deer in the headlights
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Frozen with shock, fear or confusion, so that you cannot think, speak or move.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and journalism, usually after *look*, *stare* or *freeze*. It is often humorous or mildly critical, for example about a nervous speaker or an unprepared job candidate. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *a deer-in-the-headlights look*.
examples: When the teacher called on him, he just stood there **like a deer in the headlights**.
The groom looked **like a deer in the headlights** when the DJ suddenly handed him the microphone.
On my first day at the new job, I had that **deer-in-the-headlights** look all morning.

drill.sentence: The new waiter froze {{like a deer in the headlights}} when a table of twelve walked in at once.
drill.hint: unable to move from panic (the American animal image)

entries.related: *like a rabbit caught in the headlights* — the British version; *frozen in fear* — plain description; *at a loss for words* — unable to answer.
entries.origin: From deer, which often freeze in the road when a car's headlights shine on them.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Meant as a joke or as irony, although it is said in a serious way.
entries.usage: Used about remarks, articles, ads and titles: *a tongue-in-cheek review*. As an adjective it is hyphenated (*a tongue-in-cheek title*, *it was tongue-in-cheek*); as an adverb it is often written without hyphens (*she said it tongue in cheek*). It is a useful way to explain that you were not serious: *That comment was tongue-in-cheek.*
examples: The pizza place's sign says 'Second-Best Pizza in Town,' a **tongue-in-cheek** dig at its famous neighbor.
Don't take her email too seriously; the part about firing everyone was **tongue-in-cheek**.
The film is a **tongue-in-cheek** look at life in the suburbs.

drill.sentence: Relax, he wasn't really calling you old; the birthday card was {{tongue-in-cheek}}.
drill.hint: meant as a joke while sounding serious (a mouth image)

entries.related: *deadpan* — joking with a serious face or voice; *ironic* — saying the opposite of what you mean; *sarcastic* — mocking and often unkind.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To tell someone about a worry, a complaint or a secret that has been bothering you, so that you feel relief.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often as an opener before a confession or a complaint: *I need to get something off my chest.* The object is usually *something*, *this* or *it*. The focus is on the speaker's relief, not on solving the problem.
examples: I need to **get something off my chest**: I'm the one who dented your car.
After months of silence, she finally **got it off her chest** and told her boss she was unhappy.
Writing in a journal helps me **get things off my chest** when I can't talk to anyone.

drill.sentence: Thanks for listening. It feels good to finally {{get that off my chest}}.
drill.hint: say what has been bothering me (a body image)

entries.related: *come clean* — admit something you hid; *vent* — express anger or frustration; *unburden yourself* — more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get rid of stress, anger or extra energy by doing something active or fun.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation; *let off steam* means the same and is the usual form in British English. Typical activities are exercise, sports, parties and loud music. It suggests a harmless release, and it is often an excuse for noisy behavior.
examples: After a long week, I like to go for a hard run to **blow off steam**.
The kids have been inside all day, so let them **blow off some steam** in the backyard.
The neighbors said the college kids were just **blowing off steam** after finals and didn't mean to break the fence.

drill.sentence: My dad goes out to chop wood whenever he needs to {{blow off steam}}.
drill.hint: release stress (not *let …*)

entries.related: *let off steam* — same, more common in British English; *unwind* — relax calmly; *vent* — express frustration in words.
entries.origin: From steam engines, which release extra steam through a valve to lower the pressure.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An unpleasant fact or situation that is hard to accept, but that you have to accept.
entries.usage: Used about defeat, rejection, criticism and loss, in sports, politics and personal life. It usually follows *be* or *prove*: *The loss proved a bitter pill to swallow.* *A hard pill to swallow* and *a tough pill to swallow* are common American variants.
examples: Losing the championship in the final seconds was **a bitter pill to swallow**.
For my grandfather, giving up his driver's license was **a bitter pill to swallow**.
The plant closing was **a bitter pill to swallow** for a town that had depended on it for decades.

drill.sentence: Getting rejected by my dream school was {{a bitter pill to swallow}}, but I love the college I ended up at.
drill.hint: a painful fact I had to accept (not *hard* or *tough*)

entries.related: *hard to stomach* — difficult to accept or tolerate; *a blow* — a sudden disappointment; *sour grapes* — pretending you didn't want what you failed to get.

entries.term: give someone the benefit of the doubt
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To decide to believe someone, or to assume they acted in good faith, although you can't be sure.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and at work when someone's behavior looks bad but could have an innocent explanation: *Let's give him the benefit of the doubt.* It suggests fairness and patience. The passive is common too: *She was given the benefit of the doubt.*
examples: She's late again, but her train may have been delayed, so I'll **give her the benefit of the doubt**.
On close offside calls, referees are told to **give the attacker the benefit of the doubt**.
I want to **give my new neighbors the benefit of the doubt**, but their dog barks all night.

drill.sentence: My friend's text sounded rude, but she's been really stressed lately, so I'm going to {{give her the benefit of the doubt}}.
drill.hint: assume she meant no harm (not *cut … slack*)

entries.related: *cut someone some slack* — be less strict with them; *take someone at their word* — believe what they say; *assume the worst* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To gradually accept a painful or difficult fact, such as a loss or a big change, so that you can live with it.
entries.usage: Used for grief, illness, failure, the past and big life changes, in conversation and serious writing. It describes a slow process, so it often comes with *still*, *finally*, *begin to* or *struggle to*. Do not confuse it with the business sense, *reach an agreement*: *The team came to terms with its star on a new contract.*
examples: It took my mother years to **come to terms with** my father's death.
Many former athletes struggle to **come to terms with** life after retirement.
The country is still **coming to terms with** its role in the war.

drill.sentence: After the accident, he had to {{come to terms with}} the fact that he would never play professional soccer again.
drill.hint: slowly accept (not *face up to* or *make peace with*)

entries.related: *accept* — plain; *face up to* — admit and deal with a hard fact; *make peace with* — stop fighting against something you can't change.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To talk openly about a problem or a misunderstanding so that the tension between people ends.
entries.usage: Common in families, friendships and teams after an argument or a period of awkward silence: *We need to clear the air.* It suggests an honest, direct conversation. Typical patterns are *clear the air with someone* and *a talk to clear the air*.
examples: We hadn't spoken since the argument, so I called my sister to **clear the air**.
The team held a players-only meeting to **clear the air** after the locker-room fight.
Before we plan the wedding together, I think our two families need to **clear the air**.

drill.sentence: Things were awkward between my roommate and me for weeks until we finally sat down and {{cleared the air}}.
drill.hint: talked openly and ended the tension (not *talked it out*)

entries.related: *talk it out* — discuss a problem until it is solved; *bury the hatchet* — agree to end a long conflict; *mend fences* — repair a damaged relationship.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To repair a relationship after an argument or a disagreement, usually by making an effort to be friendly again.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and personal life, usually with *with*: *mend fences with someone*. In news it often describes leaders or companies trying to improve relations after a dispute. It suggests effort and diplomacy, not just a quick apology.
examples: After the divorce, he's been trying to **mend fences** with his kids.
After years of lawsuits, the two tech giants are finally trying to **mend fences**.
I sent my old college friend a long message to **mend fences**; we hadn't talked in five years.

drill.sentence: My uncle hasn't spoken to my dad in years, but he came to the barbecue hoping to {{mend fences}}.
drill.hint: repair the relationship (not *bury the hatchet* or *make peace*)

entries.related: *bury the hatchet* — agree to stop fighting; *make amends* — do something to make up for a wrong; *build bridges* — create good relations between groups.

entries.term: get off on the wrong foot
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start a relationship or an activity badly, usually because of a misunderstanding or a bad first impression.
entries.usage: Most often about first meetings: with a new boss, coworker, neighbor or in-law. Typical patterns are *get off on the wrong foot with someone* and *start off on the wrong foot*. *I think we got off on the wrong foot* is a friendly way to restart a relationship.
examples: I accidentally called my new boss by the wrong name, so we **got off on the wrong foot**.
I think we **got off on the wrong foot** yesterday; can I buy you a coffee?
The new principal **got off on the wrong foot** with the teachers by canceling their planning time.

drill.sentence: My parents and my boyfriend {{got off on the wrong foot}} when he showed up two hours late to dinner.
drill.hint: began badly when they first met (not *a bad start*)

entries.related: *get off on the right foot* — the opposite; *get off to a bad start* — more general, also for projects or seasons.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To disagree or argue strongly with someone again and again, usually because both sides are stubborn.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and in sports and political news, with *with* or a plural subject: *butt heads with someone*, *they often butt heads*. It describes an ongoing clash of strong personalities rather than one argument. It sounds informal but not rude.
examples: My sister and I **butted heads** constantly when we were teenagers.
The coach and his star player **butted heads** over playing time all season.
The two head chefs **butt heads** over the menu, but the food has never been better.

drill.sentence: My grandmother and my mom are both so stubborn that they {{butt heads}} about everything, even how to cook rice.
drill.hint: clash like two goats (not *lock horns*)

entries.related: *lock horns* — same image, common in news; *clash* — neutral; *not see eye to eye* — milder, simply disagree.
entries.origin: From goats and rams, which fight by hitting their heads together.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Lasting anger or hostility between people or groups, usually because of something that happened in the past.
entries.usage: Common in sports, politics, business and family stories, usually as *bad blood between A and B*. It is uncountable: *a lot of bad blood*, *some bad blood*, never *a bad blood*. It suggests a long history, not a single argument.
examples: There's been **bad blood** between the two families ever since the fight over the farm.
The rivalry is full of **bad blood** after a brawl in last year's playoffs.
Years of **bad blood** between the founders finally ended with one of them suing the other.

drill.sentence: The brothers haven't spoken since their father's will was read; there's still a lot of {{bad blood}} between them.
drill.hint: long-lasting hostility (two words, a body image)

entries.related: *a grudge* — one person's lasting resentment; *a feud* — a long, active quarrel; *no love lost* — mutual dislike, often understated.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To criticize or say something with complete directness, without making it softer to protect anyone's feelings.
entries.usage: Used about critics, reports, speeches and people who give blunt feedback, often as praise for their honesty. Both *pull no punches* and *not pull any punches* are common; the first is typical in writing. The topic often follows *in*: *The review pulls no punches in its criticism of the hospital.*
examples: My writing teacher **pulled no punches**: she said my first chapter was boring and far too long.
The investigation's final report **pulls no punches** in blaming the airline for the crash.
When I asked my brother what he thought of my new tattoo, he **didn't pull any punches**.

drill.sentence: Grandma never {{pulls any punches}}: she told me my new haircut made me look like a mushroom.
drill.hint: softens her criticism (a boxing image)

entries.related: *not mince words* — speak directly, even if it offends; *tell it like it is* — describe the unpleasant truth; *sugarcoat* — the opposite, make bad news sound better.
entries.origin: From boxing, where *pulling a punch* means deliberately hitting with less than full force.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To achieve more or compete at a higher level than you would expect, given your size, experience or resources.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and politics, usually as praise: a small country, company or team *punches above its weight*. The possessive matches the subject: *its*, *their*, *his*. In dating talk it humorously means having a partner who seems more attractive or successful than you.
examples: For a country its size, Singapore **punches above its weight** in global finance.
Our little neighborhood bakery **punches above its weight**; people drive in from three towns away.
Everyone says I'm **punching above my weight** with Jenna, and honestly, they're right.

drill.sentence: Our high school team has only twenty players, but it {{punches above its weight}} and beats schools three times its size.
drill.hint: does much better than its size suggests (a boxing image)

entries.related: *hold your own* — compete successfully against stronger opponents; *overachieve* — do better than expected; *David and Goliath* — a small side against a giant.
entries.origin: From boxing, where fighters compete in classes based on body weight.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of a plan, a bill or a product: certain to fail from the very start, with no real chance of success.
entries.usage: Common in American political and business news, especially about bills that the other party will block: *dead on arrival in the Senate*. It usually follows *be* or *declare*, and the short form *DOA* is common in speech. It sounds blunt and a little dramatic.
examples: The budget plan was **dead on arrival** in the House, where the other party has the majority.
The game console was **dead on arrival**: it cost twice as much as its rivals and had no good games.
Any proposal to cancel the town's Fourth of July fireworks is **dead on arrival**.

drill.sentence: The plan to raise the speed limit near the elementary school was {{dead on arrival}}; not a single council member supported it.
drill.hint: doomed from the very start (not *a non-starter*)

entries.related: *a non-starter* — an idea with no chance of success; *stillborn* — failed at the moment of starting, more literary; *a long shot* — unlikely but possible.
entries.origin: From hospital and police language for a person who is already dead when brought in, often shortened to *DOA*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Past problems or disagreements that are now forgiven or no longer important.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, especially in reply to an apology or when someone brings up an old conflict: *Don't worry, it's water under the bridge.* It shows that you have moved on and don't want to discuss it again. *Water over the dam* is a less common American variant.
examples: We had a big fight in college, but that's all **water under the bridge** now.
When my old roommate apologized for the unpaid rent, I told her it was **water under the bridge**.
The two former bandmates now say their old feud is **water under the bridge**.

drill.sentence: I know you were upset about missing my party, but I'm not angry anymore. It's {{water under the bridge}}.
drill.hint: forgiven and in the past (not *ancient history*)

entries.related: *ancient history* — something from the past that no longer matters; *let bygones be bygones* — agree to forget past problems; *bury the hatchet* — end a conflict.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To finally decide to do something important or risky that you have been thinking about, such as getting married or starting a business.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and lifestyle writing, usually positive and a little humorous, often with *finally*. Typical plunges are marriage, buying a home, quitting a job and starting a business. *Bite the bullet* is about accepting something unpleasant; *take the plunge* is about a brave step into something new.
examples: After ten years together, they finally **took the plunge** and got married.
I'd rented for fifteen years before I **took the plunge** and bought a condo.
Many Americans **took the plunge** into self-employment during the pandemic.

drill.sentence: My parents had talked about moving to Costa Rica for twenty years, and last spring they {{took the plunge}}.
drill.hint: made the bold move they had put off (not *went for it*)

entries.related: *bite the bullet* — make yourself do something unpleasant; *go for it* — try something without holding back; *jump in with both feet* — commit fully and eagerly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take a further risk or ask for more after you have already been lucky, so that you may lose what you have gained.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as a warning: *Don't push your luck.* It is often said with humor to a child or a friend who keeps asking for more. *You're pushing it* is a shorter, more casual version.
examples: The rain had held off all afternoon, so we didn't **push our luck**; we packed up the picnic and drove home.
The team won the first two games with backup players, but the coach doesn't want to **push his luck** in the playoffs.
I've been driving on this spare tire for two weeks, and my mechanic says I'm **pushing my luck**.

drill.sentence: Mom already let you stay up an hour late, so you're {{pushing your luck}} by asking for a movie too.
drill.hint: risking what you got by asking for more (with a word for fortune)

entries.related: *push it* — same, more casual; *quit while you're ahead* — the opposite advice; *tempt fate* — do something that invites bad luck.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A chain of events in which one event causes the next, which causes the next, and so on.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and politics about failures or crises that spread: *set off / trigger / have a domino effect*. It stresses a direct sequence of causes and is usually negative. Compare *a ripple effect*, which describes wider, more indirect consequences.
examples: One canceled flight in Chicago can set off **a domino effect** of delays across the whole country.
When the bank failed, many feared **a domino effect** that would bring down other lenders.
Oversleeping by twenty minutes had **a domino effect** on my whole day.

drill.sentence: One family on our street sold their house to a developer, and that started {{a domino effect}}: within a year, five more had sold.
drill.hint: each event causing the next, like falling game pieces

entries.related: *a chain reaction* — same idea, from chemistry and physics; *a ripple effect* — wider, indirect consequences; *a knock-on effect* — an indirect result, mainly British.
entries.origin: From lining up dominoes so that when the first one falls, it knocks over all the others.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which one event has effects that spread outward and indirectly affect many other people or things.
entries.usage: Common in news, economics and business, usually as *have a ripple effect on* or *a ripple effect across / through* something. It stresses wide, indirect spread rather than a strict chain of causes. It can be negative or positive: a single act of kindness can *have a ripple effect*.
examples: When the factory closed, it had **a ripple effect** on local restaurants, shops and schools.
Higher interest rates have **a ripple effect** across the whole housing market.
One teacher's enthusiasm can have **a ripple effect** that lasts for years in a school.

drill.sentence: The drought in California had {{a ripple effect}} on grocery prices all over the country.
drill.hint: consequences spreading outward, like rings on water

entries.related: *a domino effect* — a direct chain in which each event causes the next; *a knock-on effect* — an indirect result, mainly British; *spillover* — effects that spread into another area.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: One dishonest or badly behaved person in a group, whose behavior can harm the group's reputation or spread to others.
entries.usage: Common in discussions of police, politics, companies and schools, often as *a few bad apples*. Institutions use it to defend themselves (*just a few bad apples*), and critics reply that the whole system is the problem. The full proverb, *one bad apple spoils the whole bunch*, stresses the spreading.
examples: Most of our drivers are great, but one **bad apple** who's rude to customers can ruin the company's reputation.
The whole class lost recess because of a couple of **bad apples**.
Critics say the scandal isn't about a few **bad apples** but about the culture of the entire bank.

drill.sentence: The landlord says most of the tenants are great; it's just one {{bad apple}} who throws loud parties every weekend.
drill.hint: person who spoils it for the group (a fruit image)

entries.related: *a black sheep* — a family member seen as a disgrace; *a troublemaker* — plain; *rotten to the core* — completely bad, often about a whole system.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who acts or speaks in an unpredictable, uncontrolled way and may cause trouble for their own side.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and sports news, and almost always critical. The key idea is that the person is uncontrolled and may damage their own team or party, not just opponents. Typical patterns are *be seen as a loose cannon* and *become a loose cannon*.
examples: The founder had become **a loose cannon**, posting angry rants about his own investors in the middle of the night.
Nobody wants Uncle Dave to give a toast at the wedding; he's **a loose cannon** after a few drinks.
The team traded him because he'd become **a loose cannon** in the locker room.

drill.sentence: The band kept their drummer away from reporters on the tour because he was {{a loose cannon}}.
drill.hint: a person who might say or do anything (a ship's gun image)

entries.related: *a wild card* — unpredictable, but not necessarily harmful; *a liability* — someone who causes problems for their own side; *a hothead* — someone who gets angry quickly.
entries.origin: From old warships, where a heavy cannon that broke loose from its ropes could roll across the deck and injure the crew.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person or factor whose behavior or effect is hard to predict and could change the result.
entries.usage: Common in political, sports and business analysis: *The wild card in this election is turnout.* It is neutral, unlike *a loose cannon*, which suggests danger. In American sports, a *wild card* is also a team that reaches the playoffs without winning its division, so the word is very familiar.
examples: The rookie pitcher is **a wild card**: he could win twenty games or be back in the minors by June.
Interest rates are **the wild card** in this year's housing market.
We have a good plan for the move, but my mother-in-law is **a wild card**.

drill.sentence: We've planned every detail of the family reunion; the only {{wild card}} is whether my brother actually shows up.
drill.hint: unpredictable factor (a poker term; not *unknown*)

entries.related: *a loose cannon* — an uncontrolled person who causes trouble; *an unknown quantity* — someone or something you know little about; *X factor* — a hidden quality that could decide the result.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An unofficial, invisible barrier that keeps women or minorities from reaching the top positions in an organization.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and politics. Typical verbs are *break*, *shatter*, *crack* and *hit* the glass ceiling; someone who is the first to reach a top job *breaks a glass ceiling*. It describes a problem in the system, not one unfair manager.
examples: Mary Barra broke **a glass ceiling** in 2014, when she became the first woman to run a major American carmaker.
Many women in finance say they hit **a glass ceiling** just below the level of managing director.
My aunt left her law firm when she realized she'd hit **a glass ceiling** that no amount of hard work would break.

drill.sentence: My grandmother became the first female surgeon at her hospital in 1965, shattering {{a glass ceiling}} that had stood for decades.
drill.hint: an invisible barrier to top jobs (a window material)

entries.related: *the old boys' club* — an informal network of powerful men; *a sticky floor* — barriers that keep people in low-paid jobs; *a bamboo ceiling* — a similar barrier for Asian Americans.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To use your influence or personal connections, often privately, to get something for yourself or someone else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, with a slightly critical tone because it suggests an unfair advantage. The typical pattern is *pull (some) strings to get someone* a job, tickets or a meeting. Do not confuse it with *pull the strings*, which means secretly controlling a person or an organization.
examples: My uncle **pulled some strings** and got me an internship at his law firm.
Do you think your cousin at the stadium could **pull some strings** for playoff tickets?
Reporters found that a city official had **pulled strings** to get her nephew a job with the fire department.

drill.sentence: Getting a passport in three days is nearly impossible unless you know someone who can {{pull some strings}}.
drill.hint: use their connections (not *call in a favor*)

entries.related: *call in a favor* — ask someone to repay a favor; *know the right people* — have useful connections; *pull the strings* — secretly control someone.

entries.term: can't see the forest for the trees
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be so focused on small details that you fail to understand the overall situation or what really matters.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and writing, often as a criticism or a self-criticism, usually with *can't* or *couldn't*. British English uses *wood* instead of *forest*. People also say *miss the forest for the trees*.
examples: We spent the whole meeting arguing about font sizes; we **couldn't see the forest for the trees**.
When you're planning a wedding, you can obsess over the napkins until you **can't see the forest for the trees**.
Some doctors **can't see the forest for the trees**; they treat every lab result and forget the patient in front of them.

drill.sentence: She's rewritten the first sentence of her novel forty times and still hasn't finished a chapter; she {{can't see the forest for the trees}}.
drill.hint: is too focused on details to see the whole (not *big picture*)

entries.related: *can't see the wood for the trees* — the British version; *miss the big picture* — plainer; *get lost in the weeds* — get stuck in too much detail.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: All the detailed facts about how something works or how it is done, including the small practical points.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at work and in how-to writing, followed by *of*: *the ins and outs of the tax system*. It suggests practical, insider knowledge that comes from experience. Typical verbs are *know*, *learn*, *explain* and *show someone*.
entries.pattern: the ins and outs of + noun
examples: After ten years in real estate, she knows **the ins and outs** of buying a house in this city.
My neighbor showed me **the ins and outs** of beekeeping, from choosing a hive to harvesting the honey.
Our new hire is still learning **the ins and outs** of the billing system.

drill.sentence: Before we adopted a rescue dog, a friend explained {{the ins and outs}} of crate training.
drill.hint: every practical detail of how it works (not *nuts and bolts*)

entries.related: *the nuts and bolts* — the basic practical parts; *the ropes* — how a job works, as in *learn the ropes*; *the fine print* — small, important details in a contract.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Designed to be used for everyone in the same way, without considering individual needs or differences.
entries.usage: Used mostly before a noun, with hyphens: *a one-size-fits-all approach / solution / policy*. In debates about education, health and policy it is usually critical. *There's no one-size-fits-all answer* is a very common phrase.
examples: There's no **one-size-fits-all** diet; what works for my sister makes me feel terrible.
Teachers criticized the **one-size-fits-all** testing policy for ignoring students with learning disabilities.
The new federal rules take a **one-size-fits-all** approach that doesn't suit small rural hospitals.

drill.sentence: Retirement planning isn't {{one-size-fits-all}}; a nurse and a business owner need very different plans.
drill.hint: the same for everyone (a clothing-label phrase)

entries.related: *tailor-made* — the opposite, designed for one person or need; *cookie-cutter* — made the same way every time, without originality; *blanket* — covering all cases, as in *a blanket ban*.
entries.origin: From clothing sold in a single size that is supposed to fit any wearer.

entries.term: not all it's cracked up to be
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Not as good, enjoyable or impressive as people say it is.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation when something has disappointed you or when you warn others about hype. It is almost always negative: *isn't / wasn't all it's cracked up to be*; in the past, *all it was cracked up to be* is also common. *Overrated* is a one-word equivalent.
examples: Everyone raved about that new ramen place, but honestly, it **isn't all it's cracked up to be**.
Working from home **isn't all it's cracked up to be** when your kids are home too.
Many lottery winners say sudden wealth **wasn't all it was cracked up to be**.

drill.sentence: We waited two hours to ride the famous roller coaster, and it {{wasn't all it was cracked up to be}}.
drill.hint: was less great than people claim (not *live up to the hype*)

entries.related: *overrated* — rated higher than it deserves; *not live up to the hype* — fail to match the publicity; *a letdown* — a disappointment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Having a series of successes one after another, so that things keep going well.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work and conversation, often as encouragement or a joke: *You're on a roll!* It follows *be*, *get* or *keep*: *Let's keep going while we're on a roll.* It works for small things too, like chores or card games.
examples: The team is **on a roll**; they've won eight games in a row.
I cleaned the kitchen, did the laundry and paid the bills before noon; I'm **on a roll** today.
The novelist has been **on a roll** lately, with two hit books in three years.

drill.sentence: You've answered every trivia question right tonight. You're {{on a roll}}!
drill.hint: having one success after another (not *on fire*)

entries.related: *on fire* — same, more excited; *on a winning streak* — mainly in sports and games; *hit a rough patch* — the opposite, a period of problems.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To reach the point where you are performing well, steadily and confidently, usually after a slow start.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work and reviews of shows or careers, often with *finally*, *really* or *start to*: *She's finally hitting her stride.* It describes the end of an adjustment period, not a sudden lucky success. The possessive matches the subject: *its stride*, *their stride*.
examples: The new show started slowly, but it really **hit its stride** in the second season.
After a nervous first month, she **hit her stride** as a teacher, and the kids loved her.
The quarterback **hit his stride** in the second half, throwing three touchdowns.

drill.sentence: It took me a few weeks at the new gym, but now I've {{hit my stride}} and go five days a week.
drill.hint: settled into a steady, confident pace (not *rhythm* or *groove*)

entries.related: *find your feet* — get used to a new situation; *get into the swing of things* — become comfortable with an activity; *on a roll* — having a series of successes.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Working or performing at full power, with every part working well together.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and conversation, about a team, a company, an economy or yourself. The negative often means you are tired or unwell: *I'm not firing on all cylinders today.* It is almost always in the progressive form.
examples: The team was **firing on all cylinders**, scoring on every possession in the first half.
Two cups of coffee in, and I'm finally **firing on all cylinders**.
With sales up and costs down, the company is **firing on all cylinders**.

drill.sentence: Sorry I forgot your name; I've been sick all week and I'm not {{firing on all cylinders}}.
drill.hint: working at full power (an engine image)

entries.related: *at full throttle* — at maximum speed or effort; *at the top of your game* — performing at your best; *running on fumes* — the opposite, nearly out of energy.
entries.origin: From car engines, which run at full power only when every cylinder fires.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In a situation that is too difficult for your knowledge, skills or experience, so that you cannot cope.
entries.usage: Common at work, in school and in social situations, often as an honest admission: *I was completely out of my depth.* The possessive matches the subject: *out of her depth*, *out of their depth*. *In over your head* is a close American alternative.
examples: As a biologist at a machine learning workshop, I was completely **out of my depth** for the first two days.
At the dinner party, everyone was talking about wine, and I felt **out of my depth**.
Critics said the new coach was **out of his depth** in the NFL after years of college football.

drill.sentence: My dad offered to do our taxes this year, but he was clearly {{out of his depth}}, so we hired an accountant.
drill.hint: facing something beyond his skills (not *in over his head*)

entries.related: *in over your head* — involved in something too hard, very common in American English; *out of your league* — too good or advanced for you; *a fish out of water* — uncomfortable in an unfamiliar place.
entries.origin: From swimming: being in water too deep to stand in.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: At the busiest or most active stage of an event or a period.
entries.usage: Used about parties, seasons, campaigns, construction work and events. It usually follows *be* or *get into*: *The party was in full swing when we arrived.* It is neutral and common in news and conversation.
examples: By the time we got there, the party was **in full swing** and the music was too loud to talk.
Two weeks before Christmas, holiday shopping is **in full swing**.
Allergy season is **in full swing**, and the pharmacy has run out of antihistamines.

drill.sentence: We visited New Orleans in February, when Mardi Gras was {{in full swing}} and the streets were packed with parades.
drill.hint: at its busiest and most active (not *at its peak*)

entries.related: *underway* — started and in progress; *at its peak* — at the highest point; *winding down* — the opposite, coming to an end.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To slow down or stop an activity, a process or a plan.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and conversation: *put the brakes on spending / hiring / a project*. It often suggests a sensible decision to stop something that is moving too fast. *Pump the brakes* is a related American slang phrase that tells someone to slow down or calm down.
examples: The city **put the brakes on** the new stadium after construction costs doubled.
We've **put the brakes on** our vacation plans until I find a new job.
My parents **put the brakes on** my plan to drop out of college and become a DJ.

drill.sentence: After two bad harvests, the winery {{put the brakes on}} its plans to open a second tasting room.
drill.hint: stopped for now (a car image; not *put on hold*)

entries.related: *rein in* — control or limit something; *put something on hold* — stop it for a while; *step on the gas* — the opposite, speed up.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In control of a situation, with the power to make the main decisions.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and sports, often about who has the advantage in a negotiation or a race. It usually follows *be*, *put* or *stay*: *The win puts them in the driver's seat for the title.* It is neutral or positive.
examples: With two job offers on the table, you're **in the driver's seat** in the salary negotiation.
After last night's win, our team is **in the driver's seat** for the division title.
After years of letting doctors decide, she wanted to be **in the driver's seat** for her own treatment.

drill.sentence: Houses are sitting unsold for months, so right now buyers are {{in the driver's seat}}.
drill.hint: the ones in control (a car image)

entries.related: *call the shots* — make the important decisions; *hold all the cards* — have all the advantages; *take a back seat* — the opposite, let others lead.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Not paying attention to your duties, so that problems happen without you noticing or stopping them.
entries.usage: Common in news and politics as a strong criticism of regulators, managers or officials who failed to prevent a problem. It suggests negligence rather than bad intent. It usually follows *be*: *Regulators were asleep at the wheel.*
examples: The bank collapsed because regulators were **asleep at the wheel** for years.
Parents can't be **asleep at the wheel** when it comes to what their kids do online.
Whoever was in charge of the guest list was **asleep at the wheel**; half the invitations never went out.

drill.sentence: The building manager was {{asleep at the wheel}}: the elevator was broken for a month before anyone called a repair company.
drill.hint: not paying attention to their duties (a driving image)

entries.related: *drop the ball* — make a mistake by failing to do something; *look the other way* — ignore wrongdoing on purpose; *asleep at the switch* — an older American version.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly leave an organization, a team or a cause, especially when it is in trouble, often to join a rival.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports and political news. It is slightly critical because it suggests a lack of loyalty, but it is also used neutrally for changing jobs. The new place follows *to*: *jump ship to a competitor*.
examples: When the startup ran out of money, half the engineers **jumped ship** to bigger companies.
Two of our best nurses **jumped ship** to the hospital across town for better pay.
Our lead guitarist **jumped ship** to join a more successful band.

drill.sentence: When the restaurant's head chef {{jumped ship}} to a rival across the street, half the regular customers followed him.
drill.hint: left suddenly for another place (a sailor image)

entries.related: *bail* — leave suddenly, slang; *defect* — leave one side for the opposing side, formal; *like rats leaving a sinking ship* — people deserting a failing group, very critical.
entries.origin: From sailors who left their ship before their service was over, without permission.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get through a difficult period without serious damage.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and personal life, about crises, recessions and scandals. It suggests strength and endurance, and it often comes with *manage to* or *help someone*. *Ride out the storm* is a close variant.
examples: Many small businesses couldn't **weather the storm** of the pandemic and closed for good.
Their marriage **weathered the storm** of his long illness.
The team **weathered the storm** of early-season injuries and still made the playoffs.

drill.sentence: We both lost our jobs the same year, but with help from family we managed to {{weather the storm}}.
drill.hint: survive the hard period (not *ride out*)

entries.related: *ride out the storm* — same; *keep your head above water* — just manage to survive, often financially; *hang in there* — keep going in a hard time.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of a plan, a project or a hope: to finally become real or successful, usually after a long time or a lot of effort.
entries.usage: Used in formal speech, news and writing about plans, projects, dreams and ideas. The subject is the plan, not the person: *The project came to fruition*, not *We came to fruition*. *Bring something to fruition* is the transitive form.
examples: After ten years of fundraising, their plan for a new children's hospital finally **came to fruition**.
My grandfather's dream of opening a restaurant never **came to fruition**.
It will take years for the city's new transit plan to **come to fruition**.

drill.sentence: Her plan to hike the whole Appalachian Trail finally {{came to fruition}} the summer she turned sixty.
drill.hint: was finally achieved (formal; not *… true*)

entries.related: *come true* — of a dream or wish, happen; *pay off* — bring good results; *bear fruit* — produce results, slightly more literary.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An idea, a custom or an institution that people treat as too important to question or criticize, even when it may deserve it.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and journalism, often by someone who wants to question it: *challenge*, *attack* or *slaughter a sacred cow*. It is mildly critical of the people who protect the idea. In American politics, programs such as Social Security are often called sacred cows.
examples: In this town, the high school football team is **a sacred cow**; nobody dares to cut its budget.
The new CEO wasn't afraid to challenge **sacred cows**, including the annual company retreat.
The paper's new editor went after **a sacred cow**: the daily horoscope.

drill.sentence: In my house, Saturday morning cartoons were {{a sacred cow}}: nobody was allowed to schedule anything before noon.
drill.hint: something nobody dared to question (an animal image)

entries.related: *the third rail* — a political topic too dangerous to touch; *untouchable* — beyond criticism or punishment; *a golden calf* — something worshipped too much.
entries.origin: From Hinduism, in which cows are respected as sacred and are not harmed.

entries.term: have a dog in this fight
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have a personal interest in how an argument or a contest ends, so that you care which side wins.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, mostly in the negative to say that you are neutral: *I don't have a dog in this fight.* The determiner varies: *this*, *that* or *the* fight. It sounds folksy and relaxed, so it makes your neutrality sound friendly rather than cold.
examples: You two can argue about pineapple on pizza all you want; I don't **have a dog in this fight**.
Of course my neighbor opposes the new highway; she **has a dog in this fight**, since it would run behind her house.
The referee insisted he didn't **have a dog in the fight**, even though his son plays for the home team.

drill.sentence: My two best friends both want me to say who was right, but I honestly don't {{have a dog in this fight}}.
drill.hint: have a personal stake in the outcome (an animal image; not *horse*)

entries.related: *have a horse in this race* — same idea; *have skin in the game* — have your own money or interests at risk; *stay out of it* — avoid getting involved.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Trying to organize or control a group of people who all want to do their own thing, which is almost impossible.
entries.usage: A humorous complaint, common in American workplaces, politics and family life. It often follows *like* or *be*: *Getting everyone to agree is like herding cats.* It suggests the people are independent or stubborn, not bad.
examples: Planning a vacation with six families is basically **herding cats**.
Running a faculty meeting is **herding cats**; every professor has a different agenda.
Our tour guide spent the whole day **herding cats**, trying to keep forty tourists together in the Rome subway.

drill.sentence: Getting a group of kindergartners to stand still for a class photo is like {{herding cats}}.
drill.hint: organizing people who all go their own way (an animal image)

entries.related: *too many cooks in the kitchen* — too many people involved in one task; *a free-for-all* — a situation with no order; *ride herd on* — closely supervise people, American.
